threads.thread_goal: Align on pilot scope, roles and initial household targeting approach.

messages.text: Hi team, welcome to the Community Food Support and Outreach Pilot. I've shared A1 which outlines our 6-week objective: combine surplus food redistribution with basic wellbeing checks for vulnerable households. The goal is to design a sustainable model that respects food safety, privacy and staff capacity. Before we dive into operations, I'd like to align on: (1) what success looks like for us in 6 weeks, and (2) how we identify and reach our target households. Thoughts?

Good framing. From my background in social work, I'd suggest we define success around three things: (1) consistent weekly deliveries to at least 20-30 households without safety incidents, (2) staff feeling supported and not overwhelmed by the outreach piece, and (3) households reporting they received what they needed. On targeting, we should work with community partners to pre-identify households—that's where T1 comes in. We need eligibility criteria first, then confirm interest before week one.

I agree on the safety piece—that's non-negotiable. One question: are we clear on what 'vulnerable' means in this context? I want to make sure we're not setting criteria that are too broad or too narrow. Also, 20-30 households sounds reasonable given our storage and vehicle constraints, but I'd want to confirm that with logistics before we commit.

Fair point. 'Vulnerable' in our context means households with limited access to food due to income, isolation, or health barriers—but not requiring clinical intervention. We'll refine this with community partners as part of T1. And yes, let's get logistics input on the 20-30 range. I'll coordinate with the postman/postwoman team on feasibility.

On the logistics side, 20-30 households is doable if we keep routes tight and don't add too much extra time per stop. I'll need to see the actual addresses to map it properly, but that's something we can work out once T1 is done. Just want to flag: if the outreach conversations run long, we'll fall behind. Need to keep that tight.

Understood—we'll keep the doorstep script short. That's part of T5, which I'll draft once we have the household list. The script will be maybe 3-4 questions max, takes 2-3 minutes. We're not doing assessments, just checking in.

I've been thinking about how we track all this. For T7 and T8, I'll need to set up a labelling scheme and log template that keeps household identities anonymous but lets us track deliveries and any notes. I'll draft something that avoids personal data on the labels themselves—codes only. Should have a first version by end of week.
Great. That ties into privacy, which is critical. Let's make sure the log template is reviewed by someone with social work background before we lock it in—I can do that review once you have a draft.

On success criteria, I'd add one more: zero food safety incidents. That means clear handling rules, spot checks, and everyone trained. I'll own T3—the food safety guide—and make sure it's simple enough that anyone can follow it.
Absolutely. And once we have the safety guide, we'll need a briefing session—T9—where everyone gets trained together. That's something I'll coordinate, probably week one before we start.

Okay, let me try to land the first two decisions. Based on what we've discussed: D1 is that we're aiming for consistent weekly deliveries to 20-30 pre-identified households, with zero safety incidents and staff feeling supported. D2 is that we'll define eligibility as households with limited food access due to income, isolation or health barriers, and we'll work with community partners to confirm interest before week one. Does that capture it?
Yes, that works. I'll move forward with T1 on that basis—I'll draft the eligibility criteria and coordinate with community partners this week.
Agreed. And I'll get started on T3 in parallel—the safety guide. Should have a draft by mid-week.
Sounds good. Once I have the household list from T1, I can start mapping routes. I'll need a few days to test them, so ideally that list by end of week?
I'll aim for that. Might be a draft list by Friday, then we confirm with partners early next week.
And I'll have the labelling and log template draft ready by end of week as well. That way we can review everything together early next week before we move into the operational design phase.

Perfect. So to summarise: D1 and D2 are locked. Next steps are T1 (household targeting), T3 (safety guide), T7 and T8 (labelling and logs), all with drafts by end of week. We'll review and refine early next week, then move into the operational flow design. Sound good?

threads.thread_goal: Design and agree on the end-to-end operational flow from surplus collection to delivery.

messages.text: Alright, let's design the operational flow. I've drafted a process for T2: surplus food arrives at the warehouse, we sort by type and expiry, then pack into parcels following A3 (the packing checklist). Each parcel gets labelled with a household code (no names), and then it's ready for dispatch. The key is keeping it simple so anyone can follow it. I've also aligned this with A2—the food safety guide—to make sure we're not creating extra steps. What are your thoughts on this flow?

This looks solid. One thing I'd add: we need to document the storage and rotation rules clearly. If food is sitting in the warehouse for more than a few days, we need to know what's safe and what's not. That's part of T2 as well, right? And it ties into A2.

Yes, exactly. I've got storage rules in the draft—temperature, rotation, expiry checks. I'll make sure it's aligned with food safety legislation and our equipment. Should have the full T2 doc ready by tomorrow.

I also want to flag T6—the packing checklist. That's something I'll draft, but I'll need feedback from you on what actually works in practice. Can we do a test run with a sample batch once you have the process documented?
Absolutely. Once I have T2 locked, we can do a test pack. That'll help us refine T6 and make sure the checklist actually covers what we need.

On the dispatch side, once parcels are packed and labelled, I need to know: how many per route, what time they're ready, and any special handling notes. I'm working on T4—the route mapping—but I need to understand the packing timeline first. How long does it take to pack, say, 25 parcels?

Good question. Based on what I've seen, if we have two people packing, we can do 25 parcels in about 2-3 hours, depending on complexity. But that's something we'll refine in the dry run. For now, let's assume parcels are ready by mid-morning on delivery day.
Mid-morning works. That gives me time to load and start deliveries by early afternoon. I'll draft T4 with that timing in mind. I'm assuming we do deliveries once a week—same day each week?
Yes, same day each week makes sense for consistency. Let's say Thursdays—that gives us the whole week to sort and pack, and households know when to expect delivery. Does that work for everyone?

Thursdays work for me. I'll build the routes around that. One more thing: I'll need the household codes and addresses from T1 to finalize T4. Once I have that, I can do a test run of the routes to check timings.
You'll have that from T1 early next week. And once you have the routes, I'll need to know the delivery order so I can brief households on timing. That's part of the outreach prep.

I want to make sure the labelling scheme I'm designing for T7 integrates smoothly with this flow. The household codes on the labels need to match the codes in the tracking sheet (A5) and the log (A6). I'll coordinate with you all to make sure the codes are consistent across all documents.

Good point. The codes need to be on the parcel label, in the packing checklist, and in the delivery log. Let's make sure we're all using the same format. I'll wait for your T7 draft and then align T2 and T6 with it.

Okay, so let me try to land D3 and D4. D3: we approve the collection, sorting and packing process as outlined in T2, with storage and rotation rules aligned to A2. D4: we confirm weekly Thursday deliveries, with routes mapped by T4 and packing ready by mid-morning. Does that work?
Yes, that's right. I'll finalize T2 with all the details, and we'll test it with a sample pack once the household list is ready.
Agreed. I'll have T4 done once I get the household addresses. Thursday deliveries, mid-morning packing window. That's clear.
Good. And I'll have T6—the packing checklist—ready for testing once we have the process locked. That should be early next week.

Perfect. So D3 and D4 are locked. Next steps: T2 finalized with storage rules, T4 routes mapped once we have addresses, T6 packing checklist tested. All by early next week. Then we move into the safety and privacy phase.

threads.thread_goal: Finalise safety, privacy and doorstep interaction guidelines.

messages.text: I've got a draft of A2—the Food Safety and Hygiene Quick Guide. It covers the essentials: hand hygiene, temperature control, expiry checks, cross-contamination prevention, and transport rules. I've kept it simple—one page, plain language, no jargon. The idea is that anyone can read it and know what to do. I'd like feedback before we finalize it for T3.

This looks good. One thing: I'd add a section on what to do if someone finds damaged or suspect food. That's a risk we need to cover. Also, is there a contact person if someone has a question during the pilot?

Good catches. I'll add a section on suspect food—basically, if it looks or smells off, don't pack it, and flag it to me. And yes, I'll put my contact details at the top so people know who to ask. I'll have the updated version by tomorrow.
I want to make sure this aligns with our legal obligations. Is this guide compliant with food safety legislation? I don't want us to miss anything that could expose the organisation to risk.

Yes, it's based on standard food safety regs—temperature, hygiene, traceability. I've worked with food production before, so I'm confident this covers the main risks. But if you want a formal sign-off from compliance, I can arrange that.
Let's get a quick sign-off from compliance. I'll reach out to them and ask them to review the draft by end of week. That way we can finalize A2 with confidence.

Now, on the doorstep side, I've drafted A4—the Wellbeing and Needs-Check Script. It's short: three questions about food security, any immediate health concerns, and whether they need any other support. All open-ended, non-judgmental. The whole thing takes 2-3 minutes. I want to make sure the language is right—not clinical, not patronising.
Can you share the draft? I want to review it for tone and to make sure we're not asking anything that could be misinterpreted as clinical assessment.

I'll post it in the channel now. The three questions are: (1) 'How are you managing with food at the moment?' (2) 'Is there anything health-related that's making it hard to get out or cook?' (3) 'Is there anything else we should know about that might help us support you better?' That's it. No diagnosis, no probing.

That's good. It's open, respectful, and stays in our lane. One small tweak: on question 2, maybe rephrase to 'Is there anything that makes it difficult for you to get out or prepare food?' That's slightly less clinical. But otherwise, I think this works.

Good point. I'll make that change. And I'll add a note at the top of the script: 'If someone discloses something that sounds like a safeguarding concern, don't try to handle it yourself—note it and pass it to me or the social work team.' That way staff know their limits.
I have a question: what if someone doesn't want to answer the questions? Can they just take the food and we move on?

Absolutely. The script is optional. If someone says 'no thanks, just the food,' that's fine. We're not forcing conversations. The script is there for people who want to talk, or for staff who want a framework. And if staff feel uncomfortable doing the outreach, they can opt out—we'll have someone else do that household.
Good. That takes pressure off. I'll feel more comfortable doing this if I know it's optional and I can pass if needed.

I want to flag something on privacy: if staff are taking notes during the doorstep conversation, we need to be careful about what gets written down. The log should only capture what's relevant to the pilot—not personal health details or anything sensitive. I'll make sure A6 (the log template) reflects that.

Exactly right. The log should capture: date, household code, whether they received the food, and maybe one line on any immediate needs or concerns. Nothing that identifies the person or goes into clinical detail. I'll coordinate with you on the log template.
Good. So A4 and A6 need to work together—the script guides what we ask, and the log template guides what we record. Both need to respect privacy. I'll review both once they're finalized.

Alright, let me try to land D5 and D6. D5: we approve A2—the Food Safety and Hygiene Quick Guide—pending compliance sign-off by end of week. D6: we approve A4—the Doorstep Wellbeing and Needs-Check Script—with the language tweak on question 2 and the safeguarding note added. Both will be finalized by early next week. Sound right?
Yes. I'll get the compliance review sorted and have the final A2 ready by early next week.
Agreed. I'll finalize A4 with the tweaks and have it ready by early next week. And I'll coordinate with T5 to make sure the script is documented as a guideline for the briefing.
Perfect. D5 and D6 are locked. Next steps: A2 compliance review by end of week, A4 finalized with tweaks by early next week, and both will be part of the briefing in T9. We're on track.

threads.thread_goal: Set up tracking, labelling and logging tools before the dry run.

messages.text: I've drafted the labelling scheme and log templates for T7 and T8. The idea is simple: each household gets a unique code (e.g., HH001, HH002) that appears on the parcel label, in the tracking sheet (A5), and in the delivery log (A6). No names on the labels—just the code. The tracking sheet lists all households, their assigned routes, and delivery status. The log captures date, code, delivery confirmation, and brief notes. All anonymised. What do you think?

This is solid. The codes are clean and easy to use. One thing: we need a separate master list that maps codes to actual addresses—but that stays locked away, not in the shared log. Only the delivery staff and I need to see that. Does your system account for that?

Good point. Yes, I've designed it so the master list (codes to addresses) is kept separate and secure. The shared log and tracking sheet only use codes. That way, if someone sees the log, they can't identify households. The master list is password-protected and only accessible to you and me.

I like the approach. It keeps things simple for the team while protecting privacy. One question: how do we handle the log if someone reports a concern—like if a household seems in crisis? Do we escalate that separately?

Yes. If someone flags a concern, they tell me directly—not in the shared log. I then follow up with the household and decide if we need to escalate to social services or other support. The log stays clean and factual.

From the delivery side, this works. I'll have the codes on my route sheet, and I'll mark off each delivery in the log as I go. Quick question: if I can't deliver to a household—say, they're not home—what do I note?

Good question. The log will have a 'delivery status' column: 'delivered', 'not home', 'refused', 'other'. You just mark the status. If it's 'not home', we can try again the next day or follow up with the household.
On the packing side, I need to know: does the code on the parcel label match the code in the tracking sheet? I want to make sure there's no confusion when we're packing and loading.
Yes, exactly. The code is consistent across everything. When you pack a parcel for HH001, the label says HH001, and that same code appears in the tracking sheet and the log. No confusion.
I want to make sure the log template is reviewed for privacy before we lock it in. Can I see the draft of A6?

I'll post the draft in the channel now. It's got columns for: date, household code, route, delivery status, and 'notes' (which is limited to one line—just enough to flag if something needs follow-up). No personal data, no health details.
Good. I'll review it and give you feedback by tomorrow. If it looks clean, we can finalize it.

Alright, let me try to land D7. D7: we approve the labelling scheme (household codes, no names on labels) and the log template (A6) with codes, delivery status, and minimal notes. The master list of codes to addresses stays secure and separate. Does that capture it?
Yes, that's right. I'll finalize both T7 and T8 with that approach. Should have them ready by end of week.
Agreed. And I'll review A6 for privacy and give feedback by tomorrow so we can finalize it.
Perfect. D7 is locked. Next steps: T7 and T8 finalized by end of week, A6 reviewed and approved by tomorrow. Then we're ready for the briefing and dry run.

threads.thread_goal: Review dry run results and agree adjustments and next steps.

messages.text: We've completed the dry run with 8 households over one week. Overall, it went well, but we've captured some issues in A7 (the Operational Issues Log). Main findings: (1) packing took longer than expected—about 4 hours for 8 parcels instead of 2-3, (2) one household wasn't home, (3) one parcel label got smudged, and (4) the doorstep conversations ran a bit long on average. Nothing critical, but we need to adjust. I've documented all of this in A7.
Thanks for running that. On the packing time: was it the process itself, or were there other factors? And on the doorstep conversations—how long were they running?

The packing time was partly because we were being extra careful—first time doing it. But also, the checklist (A3) had a few steps that could be streamlined. And on the conversations, they averaged about 5-7 minutes instead of 2-3. People wanted to chat, which is good, but it's eating into delivery time.

Yeah, the longer conversations were noticeable. By the time I finished the 8 deliveries, I was running about 45 minutes behind schedule. If we scale to 25 households, that's a real problem. We need to either shorten the conversations or build more buffer time into the route.

I hear you. The script is designed to be short, but people naturally want to talk more. I think the answer is: we keep the script as is, but we're clear with staff that if a conversation is going long, it's okay to politely wrap up. We can always follow up separately if needed. And we build a bit more buffer into the routes.
That makes sense. If I know conversations might run 5-7 minutes instead of 2-3, I can adjust the route timing. I'll add about 10 minutes of buffer per household. That should cover it.
On the label smudging: was it the label material, or how it was applied? I want to make sure we use a durable label for the full pilot.
It was the label material—we used regular paper labels, which got damp in the cold storage. For the full pilot, we should use waterproof labels. That's a small cost, but worth it.
Got it. I'll update T7 to specify waterproof labels. That's a quick fix.
On the household not being home: did we follow up, or did we just leave the parcel?

We left a note and tried again the next day. They were home the second time. So the process worked, but it added an extra trip. For the full pilot, we might want to coordinate with households beforehand to confirm they'll be home, or have a backup plan.
Good idea. I'll add a step to T1 where we confirm delivery times with households when we first contact them. That should reduce no-shows.

Overall, this is really useful feedback. Nothing here is a blocker. Let me summarise the adjustments: (1) streamline the packing checklist, (2) add buffer time to routes for longer conversations, (3) use waterproof labels, (4) confirm delivery times with households upfront. Does that cover it?
Yes. And I'll update A3 to streamline the packing steps. Should be done by tomorrow.
I'll revise T4 with the buffer time built in. Once I have the full household list, I can finalize the routes.
And I'll update T1 to include the confirmation step. That's a quick addition.

Great. So D8: we approve the process adjustments based on the dry run findings and confirm go for the full 6-week pilot roll-out starting next week. All adjustments will be documented in A8 (the end-of-pilot summary) as learnings. Sound good?
Yes. We're ready to go. I'll make sure all the adjustments are in place by tomorrow.
Agreed. I'll have the revised routes ready by tomorrow as well.
Same here. All updates to T1 by tomorrow. Then we're set for the briefing and the start of the full pilot.

Perfect. D8 is locked. We're go for the full pilot. Next steps: all process adjustments finalized by tomorrow, briefing session scheduled for early next week (T9), and we start deliveries the following Thursday. I'll send out a summary of all decisions and next steps by EOD today.
